summary: Gives an implementation specification for the Data Reconfiguration Service proposed in RFC 138. The service converts data between the forms used by different computers on the network. The authors come from several institutions, including UCLA, Rand, MIT, SDC, UCSB and MITRE.

eli5.summary: A detailed building plan for the translator machine from the earlier note, showing how each part should work.

subtitle: A specification for a network service that reformats data streams using stored, named forms.

tldr.problem: Application programs and consoles each need specific data formats, and the formats differ from program to program.
tldr.mechanism: A Data Reconfiguration Service sits between user and server processes. A Form Machine applies named forms, written in a small rule notation, to reformat the data stream passing through.
tldr.outcome: The DRS is described as an experiment that the authors hope will lead to a future standard service.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 166 as Unknown, with no obsoleting or updating RFCs. The text presents the DRS as an experiment that might lead to a future standard service.

sections.title: Why Reconfigure Data
sections.content:
The RFC specifies the Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS), a software mechanism to reformat network data streams. Application programs require specific data I/O formats, and those formats differ from program to program. The authors take the position that the network should adapt to each program, rather than changing every program to follow a standard. A similar mismatch arises when many kinds of consoles attach to a single service program.

The envisioned use is that an applications programmer defines forms that describe data reconfigurations, and the service stores them by name. Later, a user, perhaps a non-programmer, calls a form by name to transform a data stream. The notation is meant to be more expressive than needed for a useful experiment, yet short of a general purpose programming language.
sections.eli5: Every program wants its data packed its own way. Instead of making them all change, a go-between repacks the data for each one.

sections.title: Connections and Commands
sections.content:
A DRS implementation has modules for connection protocols, a request handler, a compiler or interpreter called the Form Machine, and file storage for forms. There are three conceptual connections: the control connection (CC) between the originating user and the DRS, where forms are defined; the user connection (UC) between a user process and the DRS; and the server connection (SC) between the DRS and the serving process.

The user reaches the DRS through the standard initial connection protocol, calling a particular socket on which the DRS always listens, and the DRS then switches the user to another socket pair. Messages on the control connection follow TELNET formats. A user supplies a six-character user ID and has commands DEFFORM, ENDFORM, PURGE, LISTNAMES, LISTFORM, DUPLEXCONNECT, SIMPLEXCONNECT and ABORT. The connect commands take a one-character method: C for already connected as a dummy control connection, I for the standard ICP, and D for a direct connection.

The DRS acknowledges each line, positively or negatively, and reports a failed or finished form with a TERMINATE message carrying the host, socket and a return code. Using and serving processes need only a minimum of modification, an NCP interface.
sections.eli5: You talk to the translator on one line to tell it the rules, and it then connects two other lines and translates whatever passes between them.

sections.title: The Form Machine Notation
sections.content:
A form is an ordered set of rules. Each rule has an optional integer label, an input stream part that describes the data to match, and an output stream part, introduced by a colon, that describes the data to emit. The Form Machine keeps an input pointer and an output pointer and advances them as rules succeed. If a rule fails to match, the next sequential rule is tried unless control says otherwise.

Terms are built from descriptors with a replication expression, a data type, a value expression and a length expression. The data types are B (bit string, 1 bit unit), O (3 bits), X (4 bits), E (EBCDIC character, 8 bits) and A (Network ASCII character, 8 bits). Comparators allow comparisons and assignment. Control options S, F and U transfer to a rule on success, failure or unconditionally, and R ends the form and returns a code to the originator.

Stated limits include binary lengths of at most 32 bits, character strings of at most 256 characters, identifiers of at most 4 characters, at most 256 identifiers, and labels from 0 to 9999. Arithmetic is evaluated left to right with no precedence.
sections.eli5: A form is a list of match-and-rewrite steps: look at the incoming data, check it fits a pattern, then write out new data in a new shape.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content: The RFC closes with sample forms: inserting a line number field for a 121 character per line printer, deleting data by not emitting it, converting variable length EBCDIC records to ASCII, prefixing a string with a length field, reordering fields (transposition), and packing and unpacking repeated characters of the kind used in HASP. For example, the transposition rule reads four fields and emits them in a different order.
sections.eli5: The examples show small recipes, such as adding line numbers, dropping a piece, or swapping the order of pieces.
